paragraphs: Understanding a vision model requires more than checking whether its predictions are correct on a collection of images. Researchers also need ways to investigate where it fails and what influences its decisions. This paper introduces 3DB, an extensible framework that uses photorealistic simulation to support that kind of testing and debugging.

The framework brings multiple robustness analyses into a common setting. It captures and generalizes analyses from earlier work, while allowing users to examine how they interact. That combination matters because separate tests can reveal individual weaknesses without showing their relationships. A unified framework provides a way to investigate those relationships as part of the same debugging process.

Across a range of use cases, the authors demonstrate that 3DB helps uncover vulnerabilities and provides insight into model decisions. They also report that insights obtained through simulation transfer to the physical world. This supports the practical value of simulated debugging in the demonstrated cases. The paper presents 3DB as a library accompanied by examples and documentation.
neurips-2022-3db-a-framework-for-debuggi.tldr: 3DB uses photorealistic simulation to uncover vision-model vulnerabilities and generate debugging insights that transfer to the physical world.

paragraphs: Finding an optimal decision tree becomes computationally difficult as datasets grow. This paper addresses classification with continuous features by rewriting tree training as a two-stage optimization problem. It then develops a specialized branch-and-bound algorithm, which searches candidate solutions while using lower and upper bounds to assess how close they are to optimality.

The main structural result is that the algorithm can converge while branching only on variables describing the tree structure. The number of those variables does not depend on dataset size. Computing the bounds splits into many small problems that can run in parallel. A sample-reduction method also determines some samples' costs in advance at each search node, reducing the remaining work.

The reported large-scale result uses more than 245,000 samples and 1,000 cores, reaching an optimality gap below 1% within two hours. Across 21 UCI datasets, the authors report average training and testing accuracy improvements of 3.6% and 2.8% on datasets exceeding 7,000 samples. These results connect the structural improvements to practical gains, with substantial parallel computation supporting the largest demonstration.
neurips-2022-a-scalable-deterministic-gl.tldr: A specialized branch-and-bound method scales optimal decision-tree training through structural search, parallel bounds, and sample reduction.

paragraphs: An anonymized histogram keeps the counts in a histogram but removes the item labels attached to them. The paper studies how to compute this object privately. Earlier algorithms in the central model of differential privacy achieved error guarantees proportional to the square root of n, for both absolute-error and squared-error measures, with privacy-dependent factors.

The authors give an algorithm for the shuffle and pan-private models with nearly matching guarantees. Its error has the same square-root dependence up to logarithmic factors and privacy-dependent terms. The procedure is notably simple: it post-processes a histogram whose counts have been perturbed with discrete Laplace noise. The contribution is that this processing provides strong guarantees in the two additional privacy settings.

The anonymized histogram also serves as a component for estimating properties of distributions that do not depend on item names. The paper gives applications to entropy, support coverage, and support size. These applications show why retaining the pattern of counts can be useful even after labels are removed: several statistical questions concern how probability is distributed rather than which labels carry it.
neurips-2022-anonymized-histograms-in-in.tldr: Simple post-processing of noisy histograms achieves nearly central-model error guarantees in shuffle and pan-private settings.

paragraphs: Machine learning models may need to meet requirements beyond predictive performance, such as fairness or stability. These requirements often concern expected behavior, but training only has access to data-based estimates. A constraint that holds on the observed sample therefore raises a further question: how can enforcing it provide a guarantee about its expected-value counterpart?

The paper addresses this gap by reformulating the constraints through calibration. Enforcing the reformulated version guarantees satisfaction of the expected-value constraint with a probability chosen by the user. The probability qualification is central: the result connects empirical enforcement to a specified level of confidence in the underlying requirement, rather than claiming unconditional satisfaction in every instance.

The resulting training problem can be handled with standard stochastic optimization algorithms. This makes calibration part of the optimization formulation, rather than only a check performed after training. The authors demonstrate the method on a classification task with a fairness requirement at test time. The demonstration shows how a desired probabilistic guarantee can be connected to constraints that a training algorithm actually enforces.
neurips-2022-calibrated-data-dependent-c.tldr: Calibrated training constraints guarantee satisfaction of their expected-value counterparts with a user-chosen probability.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether one pretrained image model can remain frozen while supporting substantially different vision tasks. Freezing the base model leaves relatively few parameters available for adaptation. That restriction is challenging when tasks differ in their inputs, outputs, and the visual information they need, as detection, segmentation, and video action recognition do.

The authors empirically examine which pretraining tasks suit this setting, how to make a frozen model more adaptable, and what happens as model size increases. They also study a three-billion-parameter SwinV2-G model to explore the performance achievable with a very large frozen base. The same base network is shared across the different downstream tasks.

The giant model reaches 60.0 box mAP and 52.2 mask mAP on COCO test-dev, 57.6 validation mIoU on ADE20K, and 81.7 top-1 accuracy on Kinetics-400. The authors describe these results as competitive. Their findings support frozen pretrained models as a promising transfer-learning approach across the studied tasks, without establishing that a single representation is universally sufficient for every vision problem.
neurips-2022-could-giant-pre-trained-ima.tldr: A giant frozen image model achieves competitive results across detection, segmentation, and video recognition using one shared base network.

paragraphs: Learning a directed acyclic graph requires finding directed relationships without introducing cycles. Differentiable tests for acyclicity make it possible to approach this discrete structural problem through continuous optimization. This paper introduces an exact, differentiable test based on a log-determinant function and the nilpotency property of acyclic graphs.

The construction uses M-matrices to accommodate the asymmetry of directed graphs, rather than the positive-definite matrix domain associated with the classical log-determinant. The authors report that their test detects large cycles better, has better-behaved gradients, and runs about an order of magnitude faster in practice than existing characterizations. These properties matter because the acyclicity test guides optimization as well as checking the resulting structure.

DAGMA combines this test with a sequence of unconstrained optimization problems regularized by the log-determinant function. The sequence resembles a barrier method's central path, and the authors prove that its limiting solution is acyclic. Experiments with linear and nonlinear structural equation models show that the approach can achieve substantial speedups and smaller structural Hamming distances than leading methods.
neurips-2022-dagma-learning-dags-via-m-m.tldr: DAGMA combines an exact log-determinant acyclicity test with an optimization path whose limiting solution is guaranteed to be a DAG.

paragraphs: Coordinating multiple learning agents is difficult when training is decentralized and useful external rewards are scarce. ELIGN addresses this setting with an intrinsic reward based on expectation alignment. Inspired by decentralized cooperation among animals, the method encourages agents to behave in ways that match what nearby agents expect.

This reward provides a self-supervised basis for collaboration without requiring external rewards or centralized training. The authors evaluate it on six tasks from multi-agent particle environments and Google Research football, comparing it with sparse rewards and curiosity-based intrinsic rewards. The reported coordination improvements involve agents dividing tasks, breaking coordination symmetries, and confusing adversaries.

ELIGN scales well as agent numbers increase in all evaluated tasks except one involving agents with different capabilities. That exception makes the result more specific than a general claim of scalability. The findings identify settings where matching others' expectations is more useful for coordination than curiosity-driven exploration. They also demonstrate zero-shot coordination, supporting expectation alignment as a practical learning signal for the studied multi-agent problems.
neurips-2022-elign-expectation-alignment.tldr: ELIGN encourages decentralized cooperation by rewarding agents for matching their neighbors' expectations.

paragraphs: A Gateaux derivative describes how a statistical quantity changes when its underlying probability distribution is perturbed. This paper studies a constructive way to approximate such derivatives using finite differences, with particular attention to causal inference. The complication is that the distribution itself must be estimated from data, so statistical estimation and numerical approximation interact.

Starting with counterfactual mean estimation, the authors establish the exact relationship between finite differences and the analytical derivative. They then derive requirements on perturbation and smoothing rates that preserve statistical benefits. The analysis extends to dynamic treatment regimes and policy optimization in infinite-horizon Markov decision processes. For the latter, the method can approximate bias adjustments even with arbitrary constraints.

The conclusions depend on the functional being estimated. Setting aside unfavorable dimension dependence from smoothing, rate-double robustness allows coarser perturbation rates for the counterfactual mean than generic finite-difference analysis suggests. The same benefit does not hold for infinite-horizon policy value. This distinction explains why a numerical derivative procedure needs statistical analysis tailored to its target rather than a single approximation rule applied everywhere.
neurips-2022-empirical-gateaux-derivativ.tldr: The paper analyzes when finite-difference approximations to distributional derivatives preserve statistical benefits in causal inference.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks models trained on available domains to perform well on different test domains. The paper finds that performance under this shift is unstable not only across independently trained models, but also along one model's training trajectory. This makes selecting a stopping point difficult: good validation performance on familiar domains may not reliably identify good performance elsewhere.

The authors propose a model-averaging protocol that improves generalization and reduces sensitivity to training randomness. It improves the rank correlation between validation accuracy within the training domains and test accuracy outside them, making validation more useful for early stopping. They then ensemble moving-average models from independent runs, obtaining further gains. A domain-generalization version of the bias-variance trade-off explains the benefits.

On DomainBed, the ensemble reaches average performance of 68.0% with a pretrained ResNet-50 and 76.6% with a pretrained RegNetY-16GF. The reported gains over ordinary empirical risk minimization without averaging or ensembling are about 4% and 6%, respectively. The contribution therefore addresses both final predictive performance and the reliability of choosing models during training.
neurips-2022-ensemble-of-averages-improv.tldr: Averaging models during training and ensembling those averages improves domain generalization and makes validation-based model selection more reliable.

paragraphs: Offline contextual bandit learning uses previously collected data to choose actions based on context. Many methods assume that deployment follows the same environmental process as data collection. This paper studies the more flexible case where the contexts encountered can change, the process generating rewards can change, or both can change.

Factored Distributionally Robust Optimization handles these two sources of shift separately. The distinction matters because changes in which contexts occur and changes in rewards are different uncertainties. The authors argue that approaches which ignore context shifts or combine both shifts can become overly conservative, especially with certain forms of reward feedback. Their factored objective is designed to mitigate that conservatism.

The paper provides estimators that are consistent and converge asymptotically, together with a practical learning algorithm. Experiments use environments based on real-world datasets, including voting outcomes and scene classification, and yield promising results. The theoretical and empirical contributions support separating the two shift mechanisms when learning robust policies, while the convergence claims concern asymptotic behavior rather than a stated finite-data guarantee.
neurips-2022-factored-dro-factored-distr.tldr: Factored-DRO separately models context and reward shifts to learn robust contextual-bandit policies with less unnecessary conservatism.

paragraphs: Hidden semi-Markov models infer an unobserved state process from observations, but their usual formulation relies on a uniform discrete time grid. That creates a mismatch for continuous-time phenomena observed through irregularly spaced events. This paper extends non-sampling inference techniques to hidden continuous-time semi-Markov chains, allowing inference to be formulated around continuous time.

The authors derive forward and backward integro-differential equations that account for the observation likelihood. They also introduce an exact integral equation for posterior marginals, which describe uncertainty about the hidden state at individual times. A scalable Viterbi-type algorithm addresses a complementary task: estimating a hidden state path rather than only separate state probabilities.

The equations can be solved efficiently using established numerical methods. The paper additionally introduces variable-step hidden semi-Markov models as a practical tool and evaluates the approaches against classical models in latent-state inference scenarios. The contribution brings both uncertainty estimation and path estimation into the continuous-time setting. Exactness applies to the stated posterior equation, while its computational solution uses numerical methods.
neurips-2022-forward-backward-latent-sta.tldr: The paper extends forward-backward hidden-state inference to continuous-time semi-Markov chains for irregularly timed observations.

paragraphs: Scientific and engineering simulations often trade accuracy against computational cost. A surrogate can combine cheap, less accurate simulations with a smaller number of expensive, more accurate ones. This paper addresses two obstacles in that combination: restrictions on how data from different fidelities must be organized and difficulty handling high-dimensional outputs.

Generalized autoregression, or GAR, extends classical autoregression using a tensor formulation and latent features. The proposed formulation accommodates arbitrary output dimensions and multifidelity data structures. It also provides tractable likelihood and posterior calculations without approximate inference. These properties make the statistical formulation compatible with complex simulation outputs while retaining a directly computable inference procedure.

The authors prove a multifidelity autokrigeability theorem and develop CIGAR, a simplified version that preserves predictive-mean accuracy while requiring substantially less computation. Experiments on canonical partial differential equations and scientific computation examples consistently outperform the compared leading methods, with up to a sixfold improvement in RMSE using few high-fidelity samples. The reported gains show how combining fidelity levels can support accurate surrogates while limiting expensive training examples.
neurips-2022-gar-generalized-autoregress.tldr: GAR combines simulations of different fidelities with tractable inference for high-dimensional outputs, while CIGAR reduces computation further.

paragraphs: Training with gradient-based methods requires choosing optimizer settings such as the step size. Earlier work showed that the step size could be learned alongside model parameters, but doing so involved manually deriving hypergradients: derivatives that describe how an optimizer's settings affect learning. This paper replaces that manual derivation with an automatic procedure.

The method modifies backpropagation so that it can compute hypergradients directly. This makes the approach easier to apply to different optimizers and to settings beyond the step size, including momentum coefficients. It also permits recursion: an optimizer can adjust another optimizer's settings, while another level adjusts the settings of that adjustment process.

The authors describe these recursive constructions as towers of optimizers. As towers grow taller, they become less sensitive to the initial hyperparameter choices, with experiments supporting this behavior for multilayer perceptrons, convolutional networks, and recurrent networks. The result addresses sensitivity to initial tuning choices rather than claiming that all choices disappear. A simple PyTorch implementation accompanies the method, making the automatic hypergradient construction concrete.
neurips-2022-gradient-descent-the-ultima.tldr: Automatic hypergradients let optimizers learn their own settings recursively, reducing sensitivity to initial hyperparameter choices.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks learn solutions to partial differential equations by penalizing violations of the equations. This paper asks whether making the commonly used L2 physics-informed loss small actually produces an accurate solution. It uses the mathematical concept of stability to examine what happens to the learned solution as the training loss approaches zero.

The analysis focuses on Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations, a class of nonlinear equations important in optimal control. For a broad class of these equations, the authors prove that stability under an Lp physics-informed loss requires p to be sufficiently large. Consequently, the usual L2 loss is unsuitable for those equations, while an L-infinity loss is a better choice.

An L-infinity objective emphasizes the largest residual rather than averaging squared residuals. Guided by the theory, the authors develop a training algorithm for this objective with an approach similar in spirit to adversarial training. Experiments demonstrate its effectiveness. The key finding is that the choice of residual loss can determine whether reducing training error meaningfully controls solution quality for the studied equations.
neurips-2022-is-l-2-physics-informed-los.tldr: For a broad class of HJB equations, standard L2 physics-informed loss is unsuitable, motivating an L-infinity training method.

paragraphs: Relative positional embeddings tell an attention model how far apart tokens are. They are also useful for length extrapolation, where a model handles sequences longer than those encountered during training. KERPLE develops a general framework for these embeddings by applying kernel functions to differences between token positions.

The construction uses conditionally positive definite kernels, a family of functions that generalizes distance measures. To preserve self-attention's interpretation in terms of inner products, the authors show that adding a constant offset transforms such a kernel into a positive definite one. Softmax normalization implicitly absorbs that offset, connecting the mathematical construction to the attention computation.

Different kernels within this family produce different relative positional embeddings, giving a principled way to derive alternatives. Experiments on three large language-modeling datasets show strong length extrapolation for the logarithmic variant. The result supports that particular variant empirically while the broader contribution is a framework for constructing positional representations. Together, the theory and experiments connect positional-distance modeling with the practical challenge of processing longer sequences.
neurips-2022-kerple-kernelized-relative-.tldr: KERPLE derives relative positional embeddings from kernels, with a logarithmic variant showing strong length extrapolation.

paragraphs: VidIL tackles video-to-text tasks using image-language models and a language model, without requiring pretraining or finetuning on video datasets. The goal is flexibility: a system should adapt to different tasks from a few examples, including tasks that require generating text rather than only matching encoded representations.

The method first translates visual content into language. Image-language models produce frame captions and phrases describing objects, attributes, and events. These descriptions are arranged in a template that preserves temporal information. A language model then receives this content together with a few example inputs and outputs, and generates the requested response. Other text, such as speech-recognition transcripts, can also enter the prompt.

Experiments cover video captioning, question answering, caption retrieval, and future-event prediction. On future-event prediction, the few-shot system significantly outperforms leading supervised models trained on large video datasets. These results demonstrate the usefulness of connecting visual descriptions to language-model prompting. They support the proposed composition across the tested tasks without requiring a separate video-training stage for VidIL.
neurips-2022-language-models-with-image-.tldr: VidIL turns video frames into textual descriptions and prompts a language model to perform varied video tasks from a few examples.

paragraphs: Learning from observation means imitating an expert when demonstrations show states but omit the expert's actions. This paper studies an offline version: the learner cannot interact with the environment. Instead, it also has recorded transitions with action labels from other agents whose quality is unknown. These two sources provide different pieces of the information needed for imitation.

LobsDICE learns through optimization over stationary distributions. Its objective compares the state-transition distribution induced by the expert with the distribution induced by the learner's policy. Matching these distributions directs learning toward the expert's observed behavior without requiring the missing expert action labels. The algorithm expresses this objective as a single convex minimization problem.

The setting is motivated by applications where expert actions are inaccessible and new interactions are costly or risky. Across an extensive collection of offline learning-from-observation tasks, LobsDICE outperforms strong baseline methods. The findings support distribution matching as an effective approach under the stated data assumptions: state-only expert demonstrations, additional action-labeled transitions, and no opportunity to collect new experience.
neurips-2022-lobsdice-offline-learning-f.tldr: LobsDICE learns offline imitation policies from state-only expert demonstrations by matching state-transition distributions through convex optimization.

paragraphs: Generalized additive models make predictions using separate nonlinear functions of individual features, combined by a linear model. This structure supports interpretation directly through the model, avoiding reliance on post-hoc explanations of a black box. However, learning many separate feature functions can require numerous parameters and become difficult to scale.

Neural Basis Models represent these feature functions using a small collection of shared basis functions. A single neural network learns the bases jointly for the task, and the feature-specific functions are built from that common collection. Sharing these components reduces the need to learn each function independently and improves scaling to high-dimensional data, especially when features are sparse.

The authors evaluate the approach on tabular and image datasets and report leading accuracy, model size, and throughput among interpretable methods. They also state that the model can represent higher-order feature interactions. The main contribution is a reusable functional representation within an interpretable modeling family: common learned components provide flexibility while addressing the parameter and computation costs of separate feature functions.
neurips-2022-neural-basis-models-for-int.tldr: Neural Basis Models share learned basis functions across features to make interpretable models more accurate and scalable.

paragraphs: Mixed-sample augmentation trains vision models on combinations of images and labels. RecursiveMix extends this idea across training iterations, using historical inputs, predictions, and labels rather than mixing only examples from the current batch. The aim is to reuse information accumulated during learning as part of subsequent training examples.

At each iteration, the method resizes the previous image batch and pastes it into the current one. Labels are combined according to the areas of the pasted regions. A consistency loss additionally aligns the meaning of repeated image content across iterations. Because that content appears at different sizes, the alignment helps the model learn representations that are less sensitive to scale.

With ResNet-50, the authors report classification improvements of about 3.2% on CIFAR-100 and 2.8% on ImageNet, with negligible additional computation and storage. The pretrained model also improves detection with ATSS on COCO and segmentation with UperNet on ADE20K, outperforming both the baseline and CutMix. These downstream results indicate that the benefits of using training history extend beyond the original classification task.
neurips-2022-recursivemix-mixed-learning.tldr: RecursiveMix reuses earlier batches and predictions in mixed-sample training, improving classification and downstream vision tasks with little extra cost.

paragraphs: Knowledge graphs contain recorded facts but usually omit many true ones. Evaluating a completion model often involves ranking a known test fact against unknown triples, effectively treating the unknown candidates as false. This paper investigates what happens when that evaluation encounters missing facts that are actually true.

Under an open-world assumption, unknown triples can include valid facts absent from both training and test data. The authors show that common measures such as mean reciprocal rank and Hits@K can then behave unexpectedly. Even with relatively few missing facts, the metrics can exhibit a logarithmic relationship with true model strength, compressing meaningful improvements into small numerical changes.

The problem also affects comparisons between models. When metric variance is considered, a stronger model can receive a lower reported score than a weaker one. The paper establishes these phenomena theoretically and experimentally and discusses possible causes and solutions. Its central implication is that benchmark rankings can reflect graph incompleteness as well as predictive ability, so small metric gains or reversed rankings may misrepresent actual progress.
neurips-2022-rethinking-knowledge-graph-.tldr: Missing true facts can compress knowledge-graph evaluation gains and even cause common metrics to rank stronger models below weaker ones.

paragraphs: Proving a conjecture often depends on finding the right supporting premises in a large library. This is difficult for language-model theorem provers because useful information may be scattered across more text than they can effectively reason over. Thor addresses this bottleneck by combining language models with automated theorem-proving tools.

The framework assigns premise selection to methods called hammers, which draw on automated theorem provers. Language models handle the remaining tasks. This division connects two kinds of capability within one proving process, allowing the system to use automated premise selection where searching a large collection is particularly important.

On PISA, Thor raises a language model's success rate from 39% to 57%. It also solves 8.2% of problems that neither language models nor automated theorem provers solve alone, demonstrating a benefit from their integration. On MiniF2F, it matches the best existing success rates with a substantially smaller computational budget. The authors provide a straightforward integration protocol intended to make Thor usable with most popular interactive theorem provers.
neurips-2022-thor-wielding-hammers-to-in.tldr: Thor improves automated proving by combining language models with hammer tools that select useful premises.

paragraphs: Classification algorithms often optimize a surrogate loss instead of directly minimizing the number of wrong predictions. This paper asks whether that substitution remains theoretically sound when an adversary can alter inputs at test time. The issue is consistency: whether optimizing the surrogate can lead to minimizing the relevant adversarial classification error.

The authors show that the adversarial setting differs fundamentally from ordinary classification. The problem cannot be reduced to independent pointwise minimization, and calibration need not be sufficient for consistency. They expose pathological behavior specific to this setting and establish that no convex surrogate loss can be calibrated or consistent in the context they study.

The paper then identifies necessary and sufficient conditions for surrogate calibration in both standard and adversarial settings. These conditions provide a starting point for designing a different class of losses. The authors also propose directions toward potentially consistent adversarial losses. That final step is prospective: the abstract establishes calibration conditions and an impossibility result for convex losses, while presenting full adversarial consistency as a remaining design challenge.
neurips-2022-towards-consistency-in-adve.tldr: The paper shows why convex surrogate losses fail adversarial calibration and consistency, and derives conditions to guide alternative losses.

paragraphs: Truly Deterministic Policy Optimization searches directly over deterministic policies without injecting exploratory noise. Its motivation is learning with long horizons and non-local rewards. When system dynamics are deterministic, avoiding injected noise can eliminate estimation variance apart from variation due to the initial-state distribution.

The method needs a way to regularize changes between deterministic policies. The authors derive a Wasserstein-based quadratic model because traditional non-metric measures such as KL divergence cannot provide the required deterministic-policy regularization. They state system-model conditions under which monotonic policy improvement can be guaranteed and propose a surrogate for estimating policy gradients. Exact advantage estimates are possible when both transitions and the policy are deterministic.

The paper introduces two robotic control environments: one with frequency-domain rewards and another with an 8,000-step horizon. TDPO significantly outperforms PPO, TRPO, DDPG, and TD3 in these environments. The findings connect a deterministic formulation to gains on the targeted control problems, while the variance and exact-estimation claims explicitly depend on determinism and the improvement guarantee depends on stated model conditions.
neurips-2022-truly-deterministic-policy-.tldr: TDPO optimizes deterministic policies without exploratory noise, with conditional guarantees and strong results on two challenging robotic control tasks.

paragraphs: Vision GNN represents an image as a graph, motivated by the difficulty of describing irregular and complex objects through fixed grids or sequences. The method divides an image into patches and treats each patch as a node. Connecting nearest neighbors creates a graph through which the model can exchange information.

The architecture has two main components. A Grapher module uses graph convolution to aggregate and update information, while a feed-forward module with two linear layers transforms node features. Together, these operations let the model combine information across connected patches and refine each patch's representation. The resulting graph-level features are used for visual tasks.

The authors build both isotropic and pyramid versions at different model sizes, exploring the graph-based design across multiple architectural configurations. Extensive image-recognition and object-detection experiments demonstrate advantages for the proposed architecture. The contribution is therefore both a representation choice and an implemented family of vision models. The reported results support graph neural networks as an effective approach for the evaluated general visual tasks.
neurips-2022-vision-gnn-an-image-is-wort.tldr: Vision GNN models image patches as connected graph nodes and learns visual features through graph convolution and feature transformations.

paragraphs: Neural-network verification seeks provable bounds on a network's outputs for a specified range of inputs. Some approaches track sets of possible intermediate values while preserving dependencies between neurons. Others formulate verification as optimization and use Lagrangian relaxations, but treating neurons independently can discard important interactions.

This paper combines the two approaches by placing zonotope representations inside a Lagrangian decomposition. The goal is to preserve useful dependency information while retaining the optimization structure of the Lagrangian method. A central result decomposes verification of a deep network into many verification problems involving two-layer networks, making smaller network blocks the units of analysis.

Those two-layer problems remain provably hard, so decomposition alone does not make exact verification easy. The authors introduce efficient relaxations that support dual-ascent optimization. Their method produces bounds that improve on both linear-programming and Lagrangian-based verification techniques in runtime and tightness. The findings show that retaining neuron interactions can strengthen verification without giving up computational efficiency in the reported comparisons.
neurips-2022-zonotope-domains-for-lagran.tldr: Combining zonotopes with Lagrangian decomposition yields faster, tighter neural-network verification bounds while preserving neuron dependencies.
